entry.title: How a soft robot inches through hard-to-reach places

media:group.media:title: How a soft robot inches through hard-to-reach places
media:group.media:description:
MIT engineers designed a robotic enteroscope that can inch through the hard-to-reach small intestine, making biopsies, drug delivery, and polyp removal easier and more precise. Inspired by snake locomotion and textured with kirigami-patterned scales, the soft robot safely navigates tight, slippery passages inside the body. (Learn more: https://news.mit.edu/2026/soft-robot-could-help-doctors-diagnose-treat-small-intestine-disorders-1028)

entry.title: Curiosity Unbounded, Episode 19 (VIDEO): Quantum Computing: Promise, Hype and Reality

media:group.media:title: Curiosity Unbounded, Episode 19 (VIDEO): Quantum Computing: Promise, Hype and Reality
media:group.media:description:
Quantum computers promise to tackle problems that are beyond the reach of today’s most powerful computers—but how close are we to making that promise a reality? MIT quantum engineer Will Oliver joins President Sally Kornbluth to explain what makes quantum computing different, why scaling quantum computers is so difficult, and what these machines could eventually mean for fields from drug discovery to materials science. They also explore the role of AI, MIT’s growing quantum ecosystem, and why Oliver believes we’ve already had our “Wright brothers moment” in quantum computing.
Transcript and show notes: https://news.mit.edu/podcast/podcast-curiosity-unbounded-episode-19-quantum-computing-promise-hype-and-reality
The Curiosity Unbounded podcast brings you behind the scenes at MIT through conversations between MIT President Sally Kornbluth and the people working in its labs and in the field. Along the way, Sally and her guests discuss pressing issues, as well as what inspires the people running at the world’s toughest challenges at one of the most innovative institutions on the planet.

entry.title: From Japan to the Moon (and back)

media:group.media:title: From Japan to the Moon (and back)
media:group.media:description:
After studying AeroAstro at MIT, Dylan Gaillard traveled to Japan through MISTI, applying his experience with autonomous systems to ispace’s lunar lander project and learning about community resilience in tsunami-impacted Kesennuma. Now back at MIT for graduate school, he continues to pursue what drives him: exploring the unknown, expanding human knowledge, and creating meaningful impact.

media:group.media:title: Helping robots avoid the unexpected
media:group.media:description:
MIT researchers developed SANDO, a new navigation system that helps robots safely navigate unfamiliar environments while avoiding moving obstacles. The system can rapidly plan and adjust a collision-free path using onboard sensors and computing, with safety backed by mathematical guarantees. (Learn more: https://news.mit.edu/2026/planning-system-ensures-robots-flight-path-will-remain-collision-free-1007)

media:group.media:title: Introducing MIT for America
media:group.media:description:
MIT has launched MIT for America, a strategic initiative to bring high-quality STEM education to all. The initiative brings together faculty, researchers, educators, students, and programs from across the Institute to democratize access to STEM learning for students across the U.S. Building on work already underway, it connects and strengthens promising approaches to reach more learners, educators, and communities. By demonstrating what's possible and sharing what works, MIT for America is designing a template for action that creates new opportunities for learners in all 50 states.
Learn more at foramerica.mit.edu.

media:group.media:title: (ᴡᴀʀɴɪɴɢ: ғʟᴀsʜɪɴɢ ʟɪɢʜᴛs) How to make robot powered by skeletal muscle
media:group.media:description:
MIT engineers have developed a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living skeletal muscle cells. Controlled using blue light, the muscle-powered robot can propel itself through water, offering a new approach to designing small, efficient bio-hybrid robots. entry.title: This robotic lab builds experiments on demand

media:group.media:title: This robotic lab builds experiments on demand
media:group.media:description:
MIT engineers have built a robotic optics lab that builds, runs, and dismantles an optics experiment, on demand. The setup centers on a robotic arm that physically arranges mirrors, lenses, and other optical components that are each set in custom-designed, QR-encoded housings. The robot arranges each component in precise alignments to direct and focus a beam of light (red laser). The autonomous system could speed up testing of high-tech materials, from solar cells and sensors to video displays and quantum technologies. This video is sped up 2x. (Learn more: https://news.mit.edu/2026/robotic-lab-runs-optics-experiments-on-demand-0917)
